meta.titre: Rédiger une lettre personnelle en anglais selon la structure imposée

source.epreuve_titre: Baccalauréat séries C-D - Épreuve d'Anglais - Cameroun - Session 2000

sections.contenu_markdown: A personal letter is one of the most frequently required formats in English exams, yet many candidates lose easy marks simply by forgetting a fixed structural element (the address, the date, an appropriate closing) rather than because of weak language. Mastering the format itself, independent of the content, guarantees a baseline of marks every time this task appears.

items: Basic vocabulary for greetings and closings in English
Ability to organise ideas into paragraphs
Awareness of formal versus informal register

sections.titre: The fixed structure of a personal letter
sections.contenu_markdown: A personal letter always contains six fixed elements, in this order: (1) the writer's own address, placed at the top, usually aligned right; (2) the date, just below the address; (3) a salutation matching the relationship with the recipient ('Dear Mum,', 'My dear daughter,' for close family; 'Dear Paul,' for a friend); (4) an opening line stating the reason for writing; (5) a body organised into two or three clear paragraphs developing that reason; (6) a closing line followed by a complimentary close matching the relationship ('Love,', 'With all my love,', 'Your loving mother,' for family and close friends) and the signature. Any word-count instruction given in the exam ('between 225 and 250 words') must be respected as closely as possible: both under-length and over-length answers are penalised, regardless of the quality of the language used.

sections.enonce_markdown: Write the opening of a letter from Veronique Tenejou (P.O. Box 65, Foumban) to her daughter, advising her on a career, in June 2000.

etapes.action: Write the writer's address, top right
etapes.justification: This is always the first fixed element of the letter

etapes.action: Add the date below the address
etapes.justification: The date always follows the address, before the salutation

etapes.action: Choose a salutation matching the relationship (mother to daughter)
etapes.justification: A close family relationship calls for a warm, informal salutation

etapes.action: Open with the reason for writing
etapes.justification: The opening line must immediately establish the purpose of the letter
etapes.resultat_markdown: 'I know you will soon have to choose the career you want to study for, and I wanted to write to you before you decide...'

sections.conclusion_markdown: With these four elements in place (address, date, salutation, opening line), the letter is correctly launched and the body can now develop the actual advice.

items.erreur_markdown: Omitting the address and date because the content of the letter feels more important under time pressure
items.pourquoi_faux: These fixed formal elements are specifically assessed as part of the format mark, independent of the quality of the content; skipping them loses guaranteed marks for no good reason.
items.correction_markdown: Write the address, date, and salutation first, in under thirty seconds, before you even start thinking about the content: they cost almost no time and secure marks immediately.

items.erreur_markdown: Using a closing formula that does not match the relationship between the writer and the recipient (for example 'Yours faithfully,' from a mother to her daughter)
items.pourquoi_faux: 'Yours faithfully' is reserved for formal letters to strangers or institutions; using it in a warm family letter creates an inconsistent, unnatural register that examiners notice immediately.
items.correction_markdown: Match the closing formula to the relationship: warm and affectionate ('Love,', 'Your loving mother,') for family and friends, strictly formal ('Yours faithfully,', 'Yours sincerely,') only for official or unfamiliar recipients.

items.enonce_markdown: Write the correct salutation and closing formula for a letter from a student to the Principal of their school, requesting permission to be absent.
items.solution_markdown: Salutation: 'Dear Sir,' or 'Dear Madam,' (or 'Dear Sir/Madam,' if the Principal's gender is unknown). Closing: 'Yours faithfully,' followed by the student's full name.

items.enonce_markdown: A candidate writes a 340-word letter when the instructions specify 'between 200 and 220 words'. Explain the consequence and how to avoid it.
items.solution_markdown: The candidate will lose marks for not respecting the word-count instruction, regardless of how good the content is, and will also have wasted valuable exam time writing unnecessary material. To avoid this, the candidate should plan the letter's paragraphs in advance, allocating an approximate number of words to each one, and check the running word count at regular intervals while writing (for instance, every fifty words).

items.enonce_markdown: Explain why the six fixed elements of a personal letter (address, date, salutation, opening line, body, closing) should be written even under severe time pressure, using the concept of 'format marks' versus 'content marks'.
items.solution_markdown: Most marking schemes for letter-writing tasks split the total mark into 'format marks' (correct structural elements: address, date, salutation, closing, appropriate register) and 'content marks' (the quality and relevance of the ideas developed in the body). Format marks are earned almost automatically simply by including the fixed elements correctly, at almost no cost in time or effort, whereas content marks require sustained development. Under time pressure, a candidate who spends the first minute securing the format marks and then writes even a shorter body still guarantees a solid partial score, whereas a candidate who skips the format entirely to save time loses marks that would have cost almost nothing to secure.

items_markdown: A personal letter always has six fixed elements: address, date, salutation, opening line, body, closing plus signature.
Match the salutation and closing formula to the relationship with the recipient: warm for family and friends, strictly formal for strangers or institutions.
Respect the word-count instruction closely: both too short and too long answers are penalised.
Secure the format marks first (they cost almost no time), then develop the content in the body paragraphs.
